prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms confined at a magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B021 to B052. The reason is the credit problem, not a lower opinion of topological insulators. In round 1 I put the conceptual breadth of a new class of matter above the cleaner attribution of the clocks. Having read the full exchange, I see that Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Kroll, each from a different angle, identify the same defect in B021: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal was the specific prediction that made Molenkamp's experiment possible, and the supplied trio leaves it out. A Nobel citation has to be defensible as written, and I cannot make the B021 trio defensible by wording alone. The lattice clock is a physically distinct achievement. A magic-wavelength lattice with Lamb-Dicke confinement cancels the light shift and the Doppler and recoil effects at the same time, and it lets very many atoms be interrogated in parallel. That is a different mechanism from the frequency comb (2005) and from single-ion control (2012), and it has been reproduced by several independent groups at roughly 1e-18. It also feeds tests of relativity, searches for varying constants and dark-matter signals, so it is more than a refinement of precision. The two-name credit, Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for the accuracy and many-body frontier, is the least contested on the shortlist. Four of eight members already prefer it and all eight name it, which tells me it is the position the committee can actually defend. The citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and its realisation, not optical clocks in general.
statement.case_against: The strongest case against B052 is the one I made myself in round 1: it comes after the 2005 and 2012 prizes and can be read as an accuracy improvement in a precision-spectroscopy lineage the committee has honoured twice. The second has also not yet been redefined, and the PTB, SYRTE, NIST and Tokyo groups built the strontium and ytterbium platforms alongside Katori and Ye, so the two-name limit does exclude real contributors. I do not think these objections are decisive. The mechanism is distinct and the physics is confirmed, so waiting for an SI decision would make recognition depend on a metrology process rather than on the discovery. The omission of the other groups is the ordinary cost of a three-person limit, and it is much smaller than the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from B021. A residual worry is that I am choosing the fallback that all of us can accept, which I have tried to avoid doing as a substitute for judgment. I have checked that the scientific reasons above stand independently of the count of supporters.

responses.point: Lindroth says the missing names are the decisive weakness of B021 and that she would support it only if a defensible three-name allocation were possible, which the supplied credit does not give.
responses.response: I have reconsidered and I agree with you. In round 1 I proposed narrowing the citation to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant, but the HgTe observation was the realisation of a specific proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, so a citation limited to the 2D effect still credits the experiment without the prediction that directed it. That also answers the chair's question to me: I judge the HgTe proposal necessary to the experimental claim, although I am recalling the history from memory. This is why I now prefer B052. I also take your point that the clock credit should be tied to the magic-wavelength scheme, and I have written my citation that way.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked B021 last because the HgTe observation followed a prediction that is not available among the credited names, and he treats the 2016 prize as close to this theme. He also names B052 as his alternative and would be comfortable with it if the committee prefers attribution certainty.
responses.response: On the first point you were right and I was too confident that the Kane-Mele concept could carry the credit alone. On the 2016 overlap I still hold that Z2 time-reversal-protected states are a distinct discovery from the quantum Hall class, but that disagreement no longer matters to my vote. On B044 I agree that the Fermi-Hubbard programme and the Zoller-versus-Esslinger question are unresolved, and I have kept B044 as an alternative. I would ask you to say whether your remaining objection to B052 goes beyond overlap and timing, since you list it as acceptable.

responses.point: Kroll argues that Katori and Ye are the least contested two names and that the other groups mostly demonstrated and improved a concept Katori proposed and first realised, with Ye's group driving the records.
responses.response: I accept that distinction between proposing and realising a scheme and improving it, and it is the reason I am comfortable with two names. I would add one condition: the citation should say what is new in physical terms, namely the magic-wavelength lattice that cancels the light shift while confining many atoms, so that it cannot be read as a reward for precision alone. I cannot check the priority among early lattice-clock proposals myself, as you pointed out in your own file, so I rely on you and Lindroth for that detail. Your disclosure of a stay in the Hall laboratory is for the chair to judge, and nothing in my reading of the evidence depends on it.

responses.point: Danielsson supports B052 over B021 on attribution grounds, while agreeing that B021 is mature and deserves to stay on the table for a future year.
responses.response: I agree with both halves. B021 should stay a live candidate, and a future committee could revisit it if a defensible allocation is found, though the three-person limit may stay a difficulty. I do not share your wish to keep WMAP (B006) as a close second, because the COBE and Planck overlap that you raised seems to me a larger obstacle than anything attached to B052. Your argument that the clock also tests gravitational redshift and varying constants is what persuades me it is a discovery and not only an instrument.

responses.point: Olsson asked how the committee should word a B021 citation that is fair to both the 2D and 3D parts without a four- or five-person list.
responses.response: I do not think such a wording exists within three names, and this answers your question as much as the chair's. Any citation covering the 2D effect and the 3D generalisation needs Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy and Hasan beside the trio. I therefore no longer advocate B021 this year. On B011, I still regard it as a serious option and I know how much atomic-scale evidence depends on it, but the Rose-Haider-Urban versus Krivanek-Dellby split is the same kind of credit problem that moved me away from B021.

uncertainties: Whether the PTB, SYRTE, NIST and Tokyo groups' contributions to the lattice-clock record are large enough that a two-name credit will be seen as unfair; I cannot judge the priority among early lattice-clock proposals.
Whether the committee regards the clock as a distinct discovery or an increment on the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which depends on how the citation is worded.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would be wiser than acting now, a question where my own judgement is not strong.

I recall the HgTe experimental and theoretical history from memory and have not verified the priority independently, so my view that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal was necessary rests on that recollection.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I work in theoretical magnetism and electronic-structure theory, which is close to B021 and may have raised my earlier enthusiasm for it; I no longer prefer it. I have no documented connection to Katori, Ye or any other credited name, and optical lattice clocks lie outside my own field, so I rely on colleagues with atomic-physics expertise for the technical priority questions.
